The integration of ChatGPT as an interactive AI mentor will significantly enhance university students' performance in complex interdisciplinary creative problem-solving tasks by providing personalized, context-driven feedback and structured guidance tailored to individual learning paths. This dual-layered interaction model incorporates adaptive real-time responses to student inputs, predefined guidance frameworks based on initial assessments of student capabilities, and collaborative engagement techniques that encourage iterative improvements in solution development. This model will be evaluated through meticulously designed metrics, including creativity scores generated by expert evaluations and peer assessments, detailed interaction logs capturing student engagement patterns, subjective measures of creativity confidence collected pre- and post-task, and qualitative insights from follow-up interviews exploring students' perspectives on the AI's role in their creative processes. A control group utilizing traditional mentorship practices will ensure robust validity and insight into comparative results.

The integration of ChatGPT as a generative AI tool within university students' engagement in complex creative problem-solving tasks—including domain-specific case studies in engineering and creative writing—will enhance performance, as measured by qualitative originality scores and quantitative solution feasibility assessments. However, this effect will be tempered by a negative correlation between the frequency of reliance on ChatGPT and students' self-regulated learning skills, specifically their self-evaluation and goal-setting abilities.

The use of ChatGPT by university students during complex creative problem-solving tasks in domains such as engineering design, literary analysis, and strategic planning will enhance their performance by improving task efficiency and the quality of creative solutions. Specifically, task efficiency will be measured by reduced completion time, while solution quality will be assessed through expert evaluation and peer review. Students with lower baseline creative problem-solving skills, assessed through standardized tests and prior coursework, will experience the most significant improvements.

University students, when engaging in complex creative problem-solving tasks, and explicitly instructed to utilize ChatGPT as an idea generation and initial solution refinement tool during the early stages of the problem-solving process (defined as the first 30% of the allotted time), will produce final solutions that demonstrate significantly higher scores in both novelty and feasibility, as measured by standardized, rubric-based expert evaluations, and achieve these results with comparable time expenditure, compared to students completing the same tasks without access to ChatGPT.

University students engaged in complex creative problem-solving tasks, when utilizing ChatGPT in a scaffolded, two-stage process – (1) initial divergent idea generation with broad, open-ended prompts from ChatGPT, followed by (2) a convergent refinement phase where students critically evaluate, select, and iteratively improve upon the initial ideas by providing specific feedback and direction to ChatGPT focusing on enhancing novelty and feasibility – will, compared to students brainstorming independently, generate a final set of ideas that are not only more numerous and conceptually diverse but also rated significantly higher in both novelty and feasibility by expert evaluators. Furthermore, this guided interaction with ChatGPT, by mirroring principles of hybrid human-AI regulation, will foster the development of students' metacognitive skills in creative problem-solving, as evidenced by improved self-reported confidence in their idea generation and refinement abilities, and a demonstrated understanding of the trade-offs between novelty and feasibility in creative solutions.

University students who utilize ChatGPT as a hybrid tool, leveraging its capabilities for iterative feedback, explanation generation, and AI-generated solution prototypes, in combination with guided modification prompts tailored to individual students' needs, will exhibit significantly improved performance in complex creative problem-solving tasks that require convergent thinking, scientific reasoning, and divergent thinking. Specifically, the integration of ChatGPT will enhance students' ability to generate novel solutions, evaluate evidence, and develop well-supported arguments. Students with lower baseline creative problem-solving skills will benefit disproportionately from using ChatGPT, as measured by the reduction in time taken and enhancement in solution quality, particularly in terms of originality, feasibility, and overall solution effectiveness. Furthermore, the beneficial impact of ChatGPT will increase over time as students become more proficient in using the tool to augment their creative problem-solving skills, and will be more pronounced when students are explicitly instructed to modify and build upon the AI-generated prototypes using a provided set of guiding prompts.

Undergraduate engineering students enrolled in a semester-long design course, who are given unrestricted access to ChatGPT for generating solutions to weekly open-ended design challenges (defined as ill-structured problems requiring iterative design thinking), will, during the first four weeks, demonstrate higher average scores on a design solution rubric (measuring solution novelty, feasibility, and elaboration, scored by two independent raters) and generate a higher diversity of design concepts based on a predefined categorization scheme, when compared to a control group completing the same challenges independently. However, after the initial four weeks and measured by the end of the semester (15 weeks in total), the ChatGPT access group will exhibit a statistically significant decrease on self-regulation subscales of the Motivated Strategies for Learning Questionnaire (MSLQ), specifically "metacognitive self-regulation" and "time and study environment management," coupled with a significant decline on solution scores on final design challenge compared to the control group which completed the same design challenges with no external tools. Furthermore, this decline in final solution scores will be correlated with the decrease in the scores of the mentioned subscales of MSLQ, while the control group maintains consistent performance and SRL skills throughout the semester. Unrestricted access is defined as students being allowed to use ChatGPT as they see fit, with no explicit instruction provided on tool usage.
